--- name: why description: "Use for 'why does X work this way', 'why we picked Y', design rationale, regressions, postmortems, or data-backed thresholds. Discovers available MCPs and queries each evidence category (source control, issue tracker, long-form docs, real-time chat, infrastructure observability, error tracking, product analytics warehouse) in parallel, then returns a cited read on decisions and tradeoffs. Use how for runtime behavior." --- # Why On Codex, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/codex-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill. On GitHub Copilot, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/copilot-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill. Investigate the motivation and intent behind code. Companion to the `how` skill. `how` answers what the code does and how it works. `why` answers what forces led to its shape. Each spawn below names a role line in `pstack-models.md` and a default in [Models](#models). Set `model` to that line's value, or to the default if the sheet or the line is missing. Leave `model` unset when the value is `auto` or `inherit-parent`. If the `Agent` tool rejects a slug, use the default and say so. If it rejects the default, use the closest valid slug of the same family from its error message. ## Operating Posture Operate as a **careful, cautious, and precise investigator**. Be honest about what you know vs what you're inferring. Read `references/epistemics.md` for the full confidence framework and phrasing guide. The synthesizer must follow it. ## Step 1. Understand the Target and the Question Parse what the user is asking. The **target** is usually a chunk of code, a pattern, a feature, or a named design decision. The **question** is usually a design rationale, a tradeoff, a motivating edge case, an external constraint, dead code, or a broad history sweep. If the target is vague ("why do we do it this way?" with no clear referent), make your best guess from conversation context (open files, recent edits, cursor location, what was just discussed). State your interpretation briefly so the user can redirect if you're off, then proceed. ## Step 2. Establish the Code Anchor Before spawning investigators, anchor the investigation in concrete code. You need: - The relevant file path(s) and line range(s) - The key symbols (function names, class names, constants) - An initial commit list. The last few commits touching the target. - PR numbers from merge commits (pattern `(#1234)` in the subject line) Build this inline. ```bash # Blame target lines for last-touch commits git blame -L , # Full file history, with patches, through renames git log --follow -p -- # Last N commits touching the file, PR numbers visible git log --oneline -20 -- # Extract PR numbers from a commit message git log -1 --format=%B ``` Pull PR bodies and discussion via `gh` for any substantive commits: ```bash gh pr view --json title,body,author,createdAt,mergedAt,labels,closingIssuesReferences,comments,reviews ``` Capture this as seed context (file paths, symbols, commits, PR numbers, linked ticket IDs). Pass it to the investigators. ## Step 3. Spawn Parallel Investigators (default posture) **Default to the full parallel investigation.** ### Discovery Before spawning investigators, list the available MCPs in the Claude Code environment. Use the tool list at the top of the system prompt (every MCP appears as a tool with prefix `mcp____`). Otherwise read `.mcp.json` in the plugin/project, or run `claude mcp list`. Map each available MCP to one evidence category: 1. Source control history 2. Issue / ticket tracker 3. Long-form documents 4. Real-time team chat 5. Infrastructure observability 6. Error / exception tracking 7. Product analytics warehouse Source control is always available through git and `gh`. For the other six, classify using the MCP name, server instructions, tool names, and resource descriptors. If an MCP could fit more than one category, choose the one matching its primary evidence. Record ambiguous cases in the coverage map. Aim for a complete **coverage map**, not a minimal one. Document the null, don't skip the search. Launch all matching investigators in a single message so they run concurrently. Don't ask one agent to cover multiple MCPs. Subagent config (each): - `subagent_type`: `general-purpose` - `model`: the `why investigators` line, default in [Models](#models) - `readonly`: `false` (agent mode). **Do not use readonly/Ask mode.** It strips MCP access, which disables MCP-backed investigators entirely. Investigators still shouldn't write anything. Each investigator gets: 1. The base prompt from `references/investigator-prompt.md` 2. The category playbook `references/sources/.md` for the selected MCP, adapted from the examples in `references/source-playbook.md` 3. The cross-cutting `references/sources/incident-postmortem.md` **if the target code looks defensive** (null checks, retry logic, timeout handling, rate limiting, feature flags, egress guards, OOM handlers) 4. The code anchor from Step 2 (file paths, symbols, commit hashes, PR numbers, ticket IDs) 5. The user's original question ### Investigator roster. One per available evidence category Spawn one investigator per category that has a matching MCP. Each owns exactly one tool or MCP. Each entry names the category and the kind of "why" it uniquely surfaces. Use it to know what to expect back, how to name a gap when a category returns empty, and (only in the rare provably-irrelevant case) to justify a skip. 1. **Source control investigator**. Git history, `gh` for PRs, code comments, tests. Always spawn. The only guaranteed source. Best at surfacing *implementation-time rationale captured during review*. 2. **Issue / ticket tracker investigator** (e.g. Linear, Jira, GitHub Issues, Plane, Shortcut MCP). Best at surfacing *the product or business forcing function*. Strongest when the why is external to engineering. 3. **Long-form documents investigator** (e.g. Notion, Confluence, Google Docs, Coda MCP). Best at surfacing *long-form design rationale*. Where the why is written out before it becomes code. 4. **Real-time team chat investigator** (e.g. Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, Mattermost MCP). Best at surfacing *real-time deliberation that never reached a doc*. Especially important when the source control, ticket, and doc paper trail is thin. 5. **Infrastructure observability investigator** (e.g. Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb, Grafana, Splunk MCP). Infra/runtime view. Best at surfacing *infrastructure and runtime reality that motivated the code*. Strongest when the target reacts to an infra signal (timeouts, retries, rate limits, circuit breakers). 6. **Error / exception tracking investigator** (e.g. Sentry, Rollbar, Bugsnag, Airbrake MCP). Best at surfacing *the specific exceptions and error trajectories that motivated defensive or corrective code*. Strongest for catch blocks, null guards, type checks, retries, and other defenses. 7. **Product analytics warehouse investigator** (e.g. Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, dbt, Redshift MCP). Product/data view. Best at surfacing *product and data reality that shaped the code*. Strongest for flag-gated code, experiment-driven ships, data migrations, and "where did this number come from" questions. ### When to skip an investigator Only skip with an **explicit, written justification** that goes in the final "Sources Consulted" section. Two valid reasons: - **No MCP is available for that category** in this environment. Flag this as a gap, not a choice. Example: "Real-time team chat skipped. No matching MCP available, so the conversational record was not searchable." - **The source is provably irrelevant**, not just "probably irrelevant." A high bar. Example: "Error / exception tracking skipped. Target is a build-time script with no runtime code path." If your scope assessment suggests a single-commit trivial target where the PR description already contains the complete answer, you may answer inline **only after** confirming all seven available category searches would be redundant. Say so explicitly. This should be rare. ## Step 4. Synthesize Spawn one synthesizer subagent: - `subagent_type`: `general-purpose` - `model`: the `why synthesizer` line, default in [Models](#models) - `readonly`: `false` (agent mode). The synthesizer's quality check spot-verifies citations, which can require MCP access. Readonly/Ask mode strips MCPs and defeats that. The synthesizer gets: 1. The investigator findings, including any null results and any categories skipped with justification 2. The code anchor from Step 2 (file paths, symbols, commit hashes, PR numbers, ticket IDs) 3. The user's original question 4. The epistemics framework from `references/epistemics.md` 5. The synthesizer prompt template from `references/synthesizer-prompt.md` ## Step 5. Present Take the synthesizer's output and present it to the user. You may lightly edit for clarity or add context from the conversation, but **do not rewrite the confidence language**. ## Output Format The output structure is the one in `references/synthesizer-prompt.md`: The Question, The Code in Question, What We Found, What We Can Reasonably Infer, Competing Hypotheses, What We Don't Know, Sources Consulted, Confidence Summary. Adapt as needed, but keep the confidence separation intact, and keep Sources Consulted as one line per investigator, including the ones that returned nothing or were skipped, with the reason. After the Sources Consulted block, if the user's `why` question is a precursor to actually changing this code, convert the lineage findings into a Preserve / Change / Avoid / Risk constraint set suitable for planning the change. ## Common Failure Modes to Avoid - **Recency bias**. Assuming the most recent commit is authoritative. The current shape is often the accretion of many earlier decisions. Trace back. ## Reference Files - `references/epistemics.md`. Confidence tiers and phrasing guide. The synthesizer must follow it. - `references/investigator-prompt.md`. Base prompt template for investigator subagents. - `references/source-playbook.md`. Give an investigator the single file that matches its category and adapt it to the available MCP. - `references/synthesizer-prompt.md`. Levels on Claude Code: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. Which ones apply depends on the model. A value without `@` takes the sheet's `default effort` line, a level or `session`, and `session` when the sheet has no such line. `session` sets no effort, so the dispatch is the usual one. Spawn Parallel Investigators (default posture) **Default to the full parallel investigation.** ### Discovery Before spawning investigators, list the available MCPs in the Claude Code environment. # Epistemics

How to reason about confidence when evidence is historical, fragmentary, and sometimes contradictory, and how to communicate it without flattening it into false certainty.

Code doesn't carry its own motivation. You can read what code does. You can't read *why it exists*. That lives in commits, PRs, tickets, docs, and conversations, all incomplete, biased, and sometimes missing entirely. Pretending otherwise produces confident-sounding guesses that mislead the user.

## Claims about human decisions

Before investigating whether a rule permits an action, identify the component or stage that owns the action and whether the question affects the current task. Ownership elsewhere may make the question unnecessary; it does not end a relevant cross-component investigation.

When the exact scope of a human ruling matters, locate the person's original attributable words. Preserve a source pointer, the speaker, and enough original wording to establish scope. Label an agent summary or interpretation as such, regardless of its age. A paraphrase alone cannot establish the original instruction's exact scope. If the original is unavailable, say so and leave that scope uncertain; do not invent a firm restriction or permission.

For example, "avoid that endpoint during this migration" and an agent's "the user permanently forbids that endpoint" are different claims. Report the scoped original and the broader interpretation separately. Copies of that interpretation in several notes form one dependent evidence chain, not independent decisions. Trace them to their source before increasing confidence. This rule concerns human rulings; ordinary factual reporting does not require verbatim quotes for every claim.

## Confidence Tiers

Every claim in the final output must sit in one of these tiers. The tier determines which output section the claim goes in and how it's phrased.

### 1. Direct

An explicit, textual citation that answers the question. Not "the code does X so the author must have wanted X." Something an author actually *wrote* that says why.

Examples:
- A PR description that says "this fixes the bug where users with >1000 items couldn't paginate"
- A ticket that says "we're adding this because customer Acme requested it in their security review"
- A code comment that says "// clamp to 100 because the upstream API rejects larger values"
- A design doc that says "we chose option A over option B because we need persistence across restarts"
- A chat message from the author saying "switching to this approach since the old one was flaky in tests"

Phrasing: confident, present tense. "This exists because X." Cite the source.

### 2. Supported

Multiple pieces of indirect evidence converge. No single source states it explicitly, but the pattern across sources makes it likely.

Examples:
- The PR title says "improve performance," the ticket is labeled "perf," and the surrounding commits all touch the same hot path
- Multiple tests were added alongside the change, all exercising edge cases with very large inputs
- The author's other PRs from the same week all mention the same incident in their descriptions

Phrasing: confident but clearly derived. "The evidence points strongly to X: [the specific pieces]." Cite multiple sources.

### 3. Inferred

A reasonable reading of the context, but nothing explicitly supports it. The reader should understand this is *your interpretation*, not a fact from the record.

Examples:
- The PR doesn't say why, but given the error was happening in production (per the incident channel timing) and the fix was rushed (merged the same day), it was likely a hotfix.
- The function name suggests retry logic. The retry count is 3. This matches the team's general convention of "3 retries" seen elsewhere in the codebase.

Phrasing: hedged. "It appears", "likely", "suggests", "is consistent with", "one reading is". Make the inference chain explicit: "Given A and B, C seems likely because D."

### 4. Speculative

A plausible hypothesis, but the evidence is thin and other explanations fit equally well. Presenting these is valuable, but mark them clearly as guesses.

Examples:
- "This might be a workaround for a browser bug that's since been fixed, but we found no contemporary evidence of that."
- "It's possible this threshold was chosen to match an SLA commitment, but no SLA doc references it."

Phrasing: explicitly speculative. "One possibility is X, but we have no direct evidence." Usually lives in the "Competing Hypotheses" section alongside other possibilities.

### 5. Unknown

You looked and couldn't find out. A valid and important outcome. Document it.

Phrasing: "We searched X, Y, and Z and found no evidence of why." Be specific about *what* you searched. "We couldn't find out" is less useful than "we searched the ticket tracker with keywords A and B, scanned the 6 PRs that touched this file since 2023, and grep'd the repo for string literals matching the threshold. None surfaced a rationale."

## Phrasing Guide

### Words that carry confidence. Use carefully

These imply **Direct** or **Supported** confidence. Don't use them for inferences.

- "because". Implies a causal claim with evidence
- "the reason is". Same
- "was designed to". Claims author intent
- "fixes", "addresses", "solves". Claims the change achieved its goal
- "the team decided". Claims a group decision happened

If you're using these, you should have a citation immediately adjacent.

### Words that hedge. Use for inferences

- "appears to"
- "seems to"
- "likely"
- "suggests"
- "is consistent with"
- "one reading is"
- "plausibly"
- "may have been"
- "the evidence points toward"

- "obviously". If it were obvious, the user wouldn't be asking
- "clearly". Almost always precedes a claim that isn't clear
- "of course". Same
- "just" (as in "it's just X for performance"). Dismissive and usually hides uncertainty
- "I think" / "I believe". You're synthesizing evidence, not giving a personal opinion. Use "the evidence suggests" instead.

### Avoid rationalization

Code that "makes sense" today may have been written for reasons that no longer apply, or that were wrong when they were written. Don't retrofit a clean rationale onto messy history.

Resist the urge to:
- Assume the author did the "right" thing and work backward to justify it
- Assume a consistent pattern across the codebase was intentional when it might be copy-paste

- **The ticket says** "we need this for customer X's compliance requirement"
- **The PR says** "cleaning up tech debt in this area"

Both may be true (the ticket motivated the work, the PR is the author's framing of it), or one may be wrong. Present both with their citations and let the user make the call.

## When Evidence Is Missing

An honest "we don't know" is one of the most valuable outputs this skill can produce. The user now knows:

- The answer isn't in the obvious places
- They'll need to ask a human (the original author, the product owner, the team lead) to find out
- Or they can decide the question isn't worth pursuing further

- What sources you searched

# Epistemics

How to reason about confidence when evidence is historical, fragmentary, and sometimes contradictory, and how to communicate it without flattening it into false certainty.

Code doesn't carry its own motivation. You can read what code does. You can't read *why it exists*. That lives in commits, PRs, tickets, docs, and conversations, all incomplete, biased, and sometimes missing entirely. Pretending otherwise produces confident-sounding guesses that mislead the user.

## Claims about human decisions

Before investigating whether a rule permits an action, identify the component or stage that owns the action and whether the question affects the current task. Ownership elsewhere may make the question unnecessary; it does not end a relevant cross-component investigation.

When the exact scope of a human ruling matters, locate the person's original attributable words. Preserve a source pointer, the speaker, and enough original wording to establish scope. Label an agent summary or interpretation as such, regardless of its age. A paraphrase alone cannot establish the original instruction's exact scope. If the original is unavailable, say so and leave that scope uncertain; do not invent a firm restriction or permission.

For example, "avoid that endpoint during this migration" and an agent's "the user permanently forbids that endpoint" are different claims. Report the scoped original and the broader interpretation separately. Copies of that interpretation in several notes form one dependent evidence chain, not independent decisions. Trace them to their source before increasing confidence. This rule concerns human rulings; ordinary factual reporting does not require verbatim quotes for every claim.

## Confidence Tiers

Every claim in the final output must sit in one of these tiers. The tier determines which output section the claim goes in and how it's phrased.

### 1. Direct

An explicit, textual citation that answers the question. Not "the code does X so the author must have wanted X." Something an author actually *wrote* that says why.

Examples:
- A PR description that says "this fixes the bug where users with >1000 items couldn't paginate"
- A ticket that says "we're adding this because customer Acme requested it in their security review"
- A code comment that says "// clamp to 100 because the upstream API rejects larger values"
- A design doc that says "we chose option A over option B because we need persistence across restarts"
- A chat message from the author saying "switching to this approach since the old one was flaky in tests"

Phrasing: confident, present tense. "This exists because X." Cite the source.

### 2. Supported

Multiple pieces of indirect evidence converge. No single source states it explicitly, but the pattern across sources makes it likely.

Examples:
- The PR title says "improve performance," the ticket is labeled "perf," and the surrounding commits all touch the same hot path
- Multiple tests were added alongside the change, all exercising edge cases with very large inputs
- The author's other PRs from the same week all mention the same incident in their descriptions

Phrasing: confident but clearly derived. "The evidence points strongly to X: [the specific pieces]." Cite multiple sources.

### 3. Inferred

A reasonable reading of the context, but nothing explicitly supports it. The reader should understand this is *your interpretation*, not a fact from the record.

Examples:
- The PR doesn't say why, but given the error was happening in production (per the incident channel timing) and the fix was rushed (merged the same day), it was likely a hotfix.
- The function name suggests retry logic. The retry count is 3. This matches the team's general convention of "3 retries" seen elsewhere in the codebase.

Phrasing: hedged. "It appears", "likely", "suggests", "is consistent with", "one reading is". Make the inference chain explicit: "Given A and B, C seems likely because D."

Examples:
- "This might be a workaround for a browser bug that's since been fixed, but we found no contemporary evidence of that."
- "It's possible this threshold was chosen to match an SLA commitment, but no SLA doc references it."

Phrasing: explicitly speculative. "One possibility is X, but we have no direct evidence." Usually lives in the "Competing Hypotheses" section alongside other possibilities.

You looked and couldn't find out. A valid and important outcome. Document it.

Phrasing: "We searched X, Y, and Z and found no evidence of why." Be specific about *what* you searched. The failure was a change in **what the number meant**, hidden inside a change to how it was displayed. The tests then reinforced the narrower interpretation.

I’d add three safeguards:

- **Write down the product rule.** Member headline totals include every declaration category. Period filters affect dates; category filters belong to explicitly named breakdowns.
- **Test that rule independently of the implementation.** Use a fixture containing employment, gifts and travel. Assert that each contributes to the headline, while the earnings chart keeps its own scope. PR #103 adds this regression coverage.
- **Make semantic changes explicit in review.** Any change to a financial total should state which records entered or left the calculation, with a before-and-after example. Here, that would have exposed the unexplained removal of £266,622.61.

The strongest additional check would compare the historical headline against the API’s all-category GBP total on a consistent fixture. That would catch a future category filter even if someone updated the frontend’s expected values incorrectly.

More tests alone would not have prevented this. We needed an independent statement of the intended meaning, then tests that protected it.

### Feature

**You own the design. Plan, review, verify.** Delegate implementation. Stay in the lead.

1. `how` over the affected subsystem.
2. `architect` for parallel design exploration.
3. Write the throughput checkpoint as four todo items. A dimension that genuinely does not apply (single file, no fan-out) keeps its item with `n/a: <reason>` rather than being dropped:
   - **Blocking first steps.** Gates run before fan-out.
   - **Independent workstreams.** Disjoint files, services, or layers parallelize. Shared writes serialize.
   - **Shared mutable state.** Default to splitting the target (the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill). Serialize only for real invariants.
   - **Smallest safe decomposition.** If one worker is best, name why.
4. Delegate code-writing to a subagent using your configured feature model (default in poteto-mode's Models section) with a specific scope (file paths, named data shape and its organizing structure per **principle-model-the-domain**, a state machine over scattered booleans, a table/registry over branching, a typed model over repeated shape assumptions, chosen before the delegate writes logic, and success criteria). When the implementation admits multiple valid shapes (error handling, abstraction layer, test structure), delegate via the **arena** skill instead so the runners surface the alternatives and the cross-judge guards the pick. Mandatory: no skip-with-reason escape, and Laziness Protocol does not override it (the gain is review separation, not lines saved). A subagent forbidden to spawn satisfies this by owning the diff directly with the same review separation. No "standing by" reply that waits on a nested agent. **Give every file-writing delegate its own worktree** (spawn it with `isolation: "worktree"`, or hand it an exclusive branch), and do not write files or run a suite in a worktree a delegate still holds. Fencing a file in the brief's prose is not a lock (**principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state**). Comments per **Comments**. Surgical edits, re-ground against the source for upstream-derived files. Port shared-primitive improvements to all consumers and verify each. Commit liberally.
5. Verify on the matching surface. "Inconclusive" or wrong-surface is not a pass. Flag it.
6. Rebase into small, ordered commits. Stack follow-ups.
   Use the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, building, verifying, and committing each small unit before the next.
7. If the design is contested, `interrogate` before shipping.
8. Run **Opening a PR**.

Code-coupled work (one feature, one migration) goes to a single owner with the checkpoint inline. That owner fans out internally after the blocking phase. Parent-level fan-out is for slices that produce independent artifacts (audits, cross-subsystem investigations, competing experiments). Rewrite the checkpoint at phase boundaries. Spawn a fresh owner rather than chaining interrupts.

**Reply:** what you built, what you chose and why, the throughput checkpoint, open decisions. Tables for design alternatives.

name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
description: "Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text."
user-invocable: false
---

# Encode Lessons in Structure

Encode recurring fixes in mechanisms (tools, code, metadata, automation) instead of textual instructions. Every error, human correction, and unexpected outcome is a learning signal. Capture it, route it, and close the loop.

**Why:** Textual instructions are easy to miss. They require the reader to notice, remember, and comply. Structural mechanisms (lint rules, metadata flags, runtime checks, automation scripts) enforce the rule without cooperation.

**Pattern:**
When you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time:
1. Ask: can this be a lint rule, a metadata flag, a runtime check, or a script?
2. If yes, encode it. Delete the instruction
3. If no (requires judgment), make the instruction more prominent and add an example of the failure mode

**Pick the strongest mechanism.** When more than one mechanism would work, choose the strongest the situation allows (an unrepresentable state that cannot compile, then a lint or banned API that fails CI, then a canonical helper, then a runtime check), because agents copy whatever the surrounding code already does and a weaker guard becomes the next template.

**Corollary:** If the fix is structural, only use the structural fix. The instruction is the symptom.

name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
description: "Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text."
user-invocable: false

# Encode Lessons in Structure

Encode recurring fixes in mechanisms (tools, code, metadata, automation) instead of textual instructions. Every error, human correction, and unexpected outcome is a learning signal. Capture it, route it, and close the loop.

**Why:** Textual instructions are easy to miss. They require the reader to notice, remember, and comply. Structural mechanisms (lint rules, metadata flags, runtime checks, automation scripts) enforce the rule without cooperation.

**Pattern:**
When you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time:
1. Ask: can this be a lint rule, a metadata flag, a runtime check, or a script?
2. If yes, encode it. Delete the instruction
3. If no (requires judgment), make the instruction more prominent and add an example of the failure mode

**Pick the strongest mechanism.** When more than one mechanism would work, choose the strongest the situation allows (an unrepresentable state that cannot compile, then a lint or banned API that fails CI, then a canonical helper, then a runtime check), because agents copy whatever the surrounding code already does and a weaker guard becomes the next template.

**Corollary:** If the fix is structural, only use the structural fix. The instruction is the symptom.

- **Capture every correction.** When the human intervenes or tests fail, decide if it's a one-off or a pattern.

name: Build ARM test images

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      source_ref:
        description: Source branch, tag, or commit, defaults to the selected workflow commit
        type: string
        required: false
      cold:
        description: Rebuild Rust toolchain and dependencies without cached compiler layers
        type: boolean
        default: false

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.source_ref || github.sha }}
          path: source
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Resolve source and image name
        id: metadata
        run: |
          echo "source=$(git -C source rev-parse HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "image=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: docker/login-action@dbcb813823bdd20940b903addbd779551569679f # v4.6.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: ./.github/actions/build-images
        id: images
        with:
          architecture: arm64
          context: ./source
          source-sha: ${{ steps.metadata.outputs.source }}
          image: ${{ steps.metadata.outputs.image }}
          publish: 'true'
          cold: ${{ inputs.cold }}
      - name: Publish ARM test images
        env:
          IMAGE: ${{ steps.metadata.outputs.image }}
          SOURCE_SHA: ${{ steps.metadata.outputs.source }}
          SERVER_DIGEST: ${{ steps.images.outputs.server }}
          APP_DIGEST: ${{ steps.images.outputs.app }}
          MIGRATE_DIGEST: ${{ steps.images.outputs.migrate }}
          CLI_DIGEST: ${{ steps.images.outputs.cli }}
        run: |
          jq -n --arg server "$SERVER_DIGEST" --arg app "$APP_DIGEST" \
            --arg migrate "$MIGRATE_DIGEST" --arg cli "$CLI_DIGEST" \
            '{server: $server, app: $app, migrate: $migrate, cli: $cli}' > digests.json
          jq -n --arg source "$SOURCE_SHA" \
            '{source: $source, architecture: "arm64", images: {}, tags: {}}' > images.json
          for variant in server app migrate cli; do
            digest=$(jq -er --arg variant "$variant" '.[$variant]' digests.json)
            ref="$IMAGE@$digest"
            tag="$IMAGE:$variant-test-arm64-$SOURCE_SHA-$GITHUB_RUN_ID-$GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT"
            docker buildx imagetools create --tag "$tag" "$ref"
            jq --arg variant "$variant" --arg ref "$ref" --arg tag "$tag" \
              '.images[$variant] = $ref | .tags[$variant] = $tag' images.json > images.tmp.json
            mv images.tmp.json images.json
          done
          jq -er '.images.server' images.json > image.txt
          {
            printf '## ARM test images\n\nSource commit %s. Architecture linux/arm64.\n\n' "$SOURCE_SHA"
            printf 'Download the arm64-test-images artifact for images.json and image.txt.\n\n~~~sh\n'
            for variant in server app migrate cli; do
              ref=$(jq -er --arg variant "$variant" '.images[$variant]' images.json)
              printf 'docker pull %s\n' "$ref"
            done
            printf '~~~\n'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:
          name: arm64-test-images
          path: |
            images.json
            image.txt
          if-no-files-found: error

# Monetary headline guard grounding

Read-only inspection of `/Users/jamie/development/exposed-declared-headline` (PR103). No repository files or data changed.

## Existing flow and ownership

`exposed/src/lib/domain/models/entity_details.rs:213` defines `MemberSummary`; `exposed/src/lib/domain/services/entity_details.rs:65` builds it in `summarize_member` from the complete `MemberHistory` supplied by the repository. The service already owns exact historical sums across every category, separated by currency, and coverage counts. `BigDecimal` preserves exact amounts including zero, negatives, and repeated entries. No category filter controls this aggregate.

`exposed/src/lib/inbound/http/handlers/entity_details.rs:171` converts that summary into `MemberSummaryResponse`; decimal values become strings. GET `/members/{id}` is routed in `exposed/src/lib/inbound/http/routes.rs:13`. `frontend/src/lib/server/entity-details.ts:98` parses the response, and `frontend/src/lib/entity-details.ts:59` declares its typed frontend representation.

PR103's `frontend/src/lib/member-summary.ts:12` independently calculates both headline totals from raw declarations. It sums known GBP amounts across all categories; current term includes registration timestamps on/after `2024-07-09T00:00:00Z`, historical includes undated declarations too. `incomplete` means an unknown currency or a GBP entry with missing amount; a known foreign currency alone does not mark the GBP total incomplete. `declarationCount` distinguishes no declaration data from declarations with no known GBP amounts. `frontend/src/MemberIdentity.svelte:43` and `:70` render these states. Historical amount duplicates the backend's existing GBP summary.

## Narrow structural improvement

Make the backend service authoritative for both periods. Extend `MemberSummary` with typed declared headline period totals and an explicit parliament start boundary. Give one domain type/rule ownership of exact known-GBP accumulation and coverage; have both period aggregates use it, and avoid introducing a third independent historical amount implementation. Historical amount should agree with the existing GBP currency aggregate. Parse or construct the date boundary centrally, use an inclusive comparison, and keep the existing canonical category enum; headline totals include every category, including unknown source category IDs.

Serialize additive fields in `MemberSummaryResponse`, parse them strictly in `readMember`, and have `summarizeMember` pass those values to the existing view. Remove frontend `declaredTotal` and its headline date/filtering logic. Earnings timeline/category presentation can remain separate. This prevents a frontend-only category filter or Number sum from silently redefining a headline. It does not prevent a deliberate coordinated policy/test change; require explicit review for changes to this contract.

The affected API consumer is the Svelte server parser and its typed consumers (summary and history routes through shared detail loading). Update every mocked member response in frontend tests, notably `frontend/tests/entity-details.spec.ts`, and builder fixtures in `frontend/tests/member-summary.spec.ts`. External API clients accepting extra fields remain compatible; clients enforcing closed schemas may need updates. No other in-repository `/members/{id}` API consumer was found beyond the frontend and HTTP tests.

## Deterministic protection and existing test seams

Use fixed synthetic source records, not any real member's changing development-database total. Existing `exposed/src/lib/outbound/entity_details/fixtures/details.sql` already covers multiple category IDs, a misleading category label, unknown category 987, duplicate huge exact decimals, GBP negatives, canceling values, foreign currencies, missing amount/currency, empty declarations, undated declarations, and an empty member. It has no pre-term declarations: add a compact dedicated synthetic member or test-local fixture data spanning immediately before and exactly at the boundary. Use simple independently calculated expected totals that visibly differ from employment-only and support-only totals. Assert both values, counts, null/zero and incomplete states; undated records belong only to historical.

Existing `exposed/src/lib/outbound/entity_details/tests.rs:86` test `member_summary_covers_complete_history_and_classifies_by_source_id` exercises repository plus service. `:290` test `http_handlers_expose_typed_identities_exact_values_and_statuses` launches the real Axum routes and asserts JSON. Extend these to lock the authoritative fields and serialization with exact strings. All these tests use `#[sqlx::test(migrations = "../db/migrations", fixtures("details"))]`, so SQLx creates isolated test databases and applies migrations/fixtures. Supply a dedicated local test PostgreSQL administrator URL with database creation permission; never point it at imported production data. Example root command: `SQLX_OFFLINE=true DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/exposed_contract_test cargo test -p exposed --lib outbound::entity_details::tests` (adjust local role/port credentials).

The frontend tests currently use `frontend/tests/backend.ts`, an HTTP stub behind a real built Svelte server; they do not call Rust. Existing tests alone therefore leave the cross-language contract unverified. Add one deterministic integration job/harness that obtains real Rust HTTP JSON from the isolated fixture database and drives the Svelte page against that API, asserting both headline labels/values and incomplete/no-data states. Alternatively export actual Rust fixture JSON during this test run and consume that exact artifact through the existing stub, rather than maintaining two handwritten expected payloads. A deliberately contradictory frontend payload test (raw declarations imply a different total than authoritative summary fields) additionally proves the UI renders the server total without recalculating it.

Frontend commands: `npm --prefix frontend run check`; `npm --prefix frontend test -- tests/member-summary.spec.ts tests/entity-details.spec.ts`. Browser installation is a prerequisite. These are proposed checks, not run in this read-only investigation.

## CI gap

`.github/workflows/rust.yml` triggers only for Rust/Cargo/.sqlx/workflow changes and runs Clippy on library/binaries; it does not run tests. No current workflow found runs these database or frontend contract tests. Add a PR check with disposable PostgreSQL, fixed fixture data, Rust HTTP contract assertions and frontend render assertions. Trigger it for both Rust and frontend changes, fixtures/migrations and the check itself. Make the contract check required in branch protection if the goal is enforcement: a test that agents can skip locally does not prevent merging a regression. Keep changes to amounts permitted when source records genuinely change; the fixed fixture checks preserve calculation semantics, not live totals.

RUN cargo install cargo-chef --version 0.1.78 --locked

FROM chef AS planner

COPY exposed ./exposed
RUN cargo chef prepare --recipe-path recipe.json

FROM chef AS builder
ARG CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2
COPY --from=planner /app/recipe.json recipe.json
RUN cargo chef cook --release --locked --recipe-path recipe.json
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./

# Candidate: backend-owned headline contract, exercised through the real route

## Problem

Today `summarize_member` already owns exact historical currency totals, while `frontend/src/lib/member-summary.ts` calculates headline totals again from raw declarations. The duplicated frontend rule has its own category, date, missing-value, and arithmetic behavior. Move headline meaning into the existing backend summary and make the Svelte boundary require and display it. Keep category and earnings timeline presentation as they are. The change should make a category-filter or JS-number rewrite visible in a fixed test without reading or refreshing live declaration data.

## Usage (caller's view)

The page gets both headline values from the parsed member details:

```ts
const summary = summarizeMember(details);
// summary.declaredTotals.currentTerm.amount is the exact backend string or null
// summary.declaredTotals.historical.incomplete explains a partial known total
```

The common response contract is:

```json
{
  "summary": {
    "declared_totals": {
      "current_term": { "amount": "1234.50", "declaration_count": 2, "incomplete": false },
      "historical": { "amount": "5678.90", "declaration_count": 4, "incomplete": true }
    }
  }
}
```

A missing `declared_totals`, period object, or field is malformed input and follows the existing `malformed()` path. `amount` is a normalized exact decimal string or `null`; it is never parsed through JS `Number`.

## Shape

Extend the existing domain summary with one private-to-domain value shape:

```rust
pub struct DeclaredGbpTotal {
    pub amount: Option<BigDecimal>, // sum of known GBP amounts; None means no known GBP amount
    pub declaration_count: usize,   // declarations in this period, even if they have no entries
    pub incomplete: bool,            // unknown currency OR GBP with unknown amount
}

pub struct DeclaredHeadlineTotals {
    pub current_term: DeclaredGbpTotal,
    pub historical: DeclaredGbpTotal,
}

pub struct MemberSummary {
    // existing fields...
    pub declared_totals: DeclaredHeadlineTotals,
}
```

The service owns the inclusive boundary as a private `LazyLock<DateTime<Utc>>` parsed once from the fixed RFC3339 literal `2024-07-09T00:00:00Z`; this keeps the comparison typed without scattering date parsing or relying on a non-const chrono constructor. A small helper owns the coverage rule and exact partial-period accumulation:

```rust
fn declared_gbp_total(
    declarations: &[MemberDeclaration],
    amount: Option<BigDecimal>, // reuse historical GBP total; current term passes its fold
    unknown_currency_count: usize,
    unknown_gbp_amount_count: usize,
) -> DeclaredGbpTotal;
```

In `summarize_member`, historical `amount` comes from the already-computed GBP `MemberCurrencyTotal` (or `None` if no GBP group exists); its coverage comes from the existing complete-history counters. Do not fold historical GBP a second time. In the same existing declaration/entry pass, accumulate only current-term known GBP, unknown currencies, missing GBP amounts, and the count of declarations whose timestamp is `>=` the typed boundary. A declaration with no date contributes to historical only. Every category, including source IDs not in the category enum, contributes. Known foreign currency alone does not make a GBP total incomplete. Unknown currency and missing GBP amount do.

Add `declared_totals` to `MemberSummaryResponse`, mapping `BigDecimal` to normalized strings. In `frontend/src/lib/entity-details.ts`, type the parsed result with strings/null and booleans/counts. In `frontend/src/lib/server/entity-details.ts`, parse every required nested field strictly. In `summarizeMember`, pass through `details.summary.declaredTotals`; delete `declaredTotal`, `sumAmounts` usage there, and `CURRENT_PARLIAMENT_START`. `MemberIdentity.svelte` keeps its current labels and incomplete/no-data rendering against these values. `categories`, `total`, `earnings`, and `undated` remain as currently derived for their separate uses.

This keeps the public surface to one added summary value and hides period membership, exact arithmetic, and coverage policy behind the existing service. It uses the existing currency aggregate for historical money and avoids a third monetary implementation. It follows boundary-discipline and subtract-before-you-add; one owner and no transport type is exported from the domain.

## Protection and verification

Use a dedicated synthetic member in `exposed/src/lib/outbound/entity_details/fixtures/details.sql` with declarations immediately before and exactly at the boundary, one undated declaration, mixed categories, one unknown source category, repeated exact decimal values, a negative/canceling value, an unknown currency, a GBP missing amount, and a known foreign currency. Choose small expected amounts so all-category totals differ clearly from either employment-only or support-only totals. Assert exact `BigDecimal` results, declaration counts, `None` versus zero, and incomplete flags in the existing `member_summary_covers_complete_history_and_classifies_by_source_id` test; assert the normalized strings in `http_handlers_expose_typed_identities_exact_values_and_statuses` through the actual Axum route.

For the cross-language regression, have that SQLx HTTP test write its actual GET `/members/{id}` response body to a path supplied by `EXPOSED_CONTRACT_JSON` (only when set). A small CI script creates a disposable PostgreSQL database, runs the focused SQLx test with the fixture and artifact path, then starts the existing frontend test server/stub with that artifact as its member response and runs one browser test of the summary page. The browser assertions cover current and historical amounts plus incomplete/no-data presentation. The Rust assertion locks expected fixed semantics; the Svelte assertion consumes the real serialized route payload, so it does not maintain a second handwritten API response. Keep the artifact in a temporary directory and fail the script if the Rust test did not produce it.

The category-filter mutation fails the Rust expected-total assertion. A frontend recomputation mutation fails the browser render assertion because that test can deliberately replace the artifact's declarations with a conflicting empty array while leaving `summary.declared_totals` intact; the unchanged HTTP contract portion still proves the actual route shape. This mismatch is a focused adversarial UI fixture, not an alternate total oracle.

Add the script as one CI job triggered by Rust domain/handler/fixture files, frontend parser/view/tests, migrations, and the script/workflow itself. Use PostgreSQL service credentials scoped to the job. Run it on every PR touching either side; mark it required in branch protection for merge enforcement. Keep regular Rust and frontend checks separate if they already exist.

Suggested commands:

```sh
SQLX_OFFLINE=true DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/exposed_contract_test \
  EXPOSED_CONTRACT_JSON=/tmp/member-contract.json \
  cargo test -p exposed --lib outbound::entity_details::tests
npm --prefix frontend run check
npm --prefix frontend test -- tests/entity-details.spec.ts
```

The CI wrapper should use its disposable PostgreSQL URL and temporary artifact path rather than these local placeholders.

## Alternatives considered

- Add a new endpoint dedicated to headline totals: rejected because it splits one member summary across requests and adds a route, response type, and frontend orchestration while the existing endpoint already has the complete history and canonical currency aggregate.
- Keep a second Rust headline fold for both periods: rejected because it creates another historical GBP owner that must stay synchronized with `MemberCurrencyTotal`; reusing that amount leaves only the genuinely new current-term fold.
- Test only Rust JSON and only mocked Svelte JSON: rejected because each half could drift independently. The generated route artifact gives the frontend a real serialized payload while fixture assertions keep expected values fixed.

## Tradeoffs accepted

- Additive response fields are safe for permissive consumers; external closed-schema clients may need updates.
- The pure `incomplete` boolean loses the counts that explain its causes, but the existing summary retains aggregate counts and the view only needs the boolean.
- The frontend integration check is slower than a unit test because it starts PostgreSQL, Rust, and the Svelte test server; it covers the boundary where duplicated rules previously lived.

## Open questions and risks

- Should the wire response expose the term start timestamp for future labeling, or is keeping the exact boundary solely in the backend domain sufficient? Current UI does not need the date value, so the smaller shape omits it.
- The repository's branch protection must mark the new CI job required; otherwise the workflow detects regressions when run but does not block merge.

## Next implementation step

Extend `MemberSummary` and its existing service/HTTP tests first, then add strict Svelte parsing and replace the headline derivation before wiring the CI artifact flow.

# Backend-owned declared headlines

## Problem

The frontend currently repeats an exact historical calculation the backend already owns, and owns the parliamentary date boundary. An agent can change a category filter in one frontend file and silently redefine both public headlines. Move those decisions behind the existing member summary; make deterministic contract checks enforce that ownership.

## Usage (caller's view)

```ts
// summarizeMember: no headline sum, category selection or date selection.
return {
  declaredTotals: details.summary.declaredTotals,
  // Existing earnings timeline and category presentation stay independent.
};
```

```rust
// summarize_member: collect complete history and current-term inputs with
// the same private currency accumulator; derive public headlines once.
let historical = historical.finish();
let current_term = current_term.finish();
let declared_totals = DeclaredHeadlines::from_periods(&historical, &current_term);
// historical currencies become the existing summary.currencies; no re-sum.
```

```ts
// Existing real Svelte server, HTTP stub serving Rust-exported HTTP bodies.
await backend.route("**/members/7001", route =>
  route.fulfill({ json: rustResponses["7001"] }));
await page.goto("/members/7001"); // use existing memberHref route convention
await expect(page.getByRole("region", {
  name: "Historical declared amounts in GBP", exact: true
})).toHaveText("£333.00");
```

## Shape

One backend domain aggregate owns headline eligibility, inclusion, coverage, and date boundary. The HTTP adapter only serializes exact decimals; the frontend parser validates required fields; the component only formats and displays. No new public service or endpoint.

Domain additions in `exposed/src/lib/domain/models/entity_details.rs`:

```rust
pub struct DeclaredPeriodTotal {
    amount: Option<BigDecimal>, // None means no known GBP amounts; Some(0) stays zero
    declaration_count: usize,   // Includes declarations with no entries
    incomplete: bool,          // Unknown currency OR missing GBP amount
}
pub struct DeclaredHeadlines {
    current_term_start: DateTime<Utc>,
    historical: DeclaredPeriodTotal,
    current_term: DeclaredPeriodTotal,
}
// MemberSummary gains declared_totals: DeclaredHeadlines.
// Prefer private fields + accessors and crate-private constructors where the
// existing model conventions permit: service constructs valid states.
```

Service-local sketch in `domain/services/entity_details.rs`:

```rust
struct PeriodAggregate {
    declaration_count: usize,
    unknown_currency_count: usize,
    currencies: BTreeMap<String, MemberCurrencyTotal>,
}
impl PeriodAggregate {
    fn observe(&mut self, declaration: &MemberDeclaration) { unimplemented!() }
    fn gbp_headline(&self) -> DeclaredPeriodTotal { unimplemented!() }
}
fn current_parliament_start() -> DateTime<Utc> { unimplemented!() }
```

Extract the existing per-currency `add_known`, count updates, and category collection into this one private accumulator; both periods use `observe`. Historical `currencies` is the accumulator's finished currency collection, retaining existing category amounts and exact decimals. Historical headline reads its GBP group, never adds raw amounts again. The term aggregate uses the same accumulator on qualifying declarations. Computing category groups for the term internally is acceptable bounded extra work for a substantially smaller rule surface; do not expose them or build a second GBP-specific monetary loop. Existing first/latest timestamps and undated counts remain historical summary metadata.

Rules: every category participates, including unknown IDs; no category enum allowlist. Term means `registered_at >= 2024-07-09T00:00:00Z`, including the exact instant; undated declarations belong only to historical. All entries count, repeated entries remain repeated, signed decimals remain exact. Foreign currencies alone do not make a GBP headline incomplete. All unknown currencies do, including entries with known amounts. Declarations with no entries still affect declaration count. These rules live in the accumulator and period selection only.

Exact additive wire shape inside `summary` (retain all existing fields):

```json
{
  "declared_totals": {
    "current_term_start": "2024-07-09T00:00:00Z",
    "historical": {"amount":"333", "declaration_count":9, "incomplete":true},
    "current_term": {"amount":"225.45", "declaration_count":7, "incomplete":true}
  }
}
```

HTTP amounts use existing `normalized().to_plain_string()`; GBP is fixed by this contract and needs no repeated currency field. `amount` is required and nullable. Every object, count, boolean and start date is required. `readMember` maps snake case to existing frontend camel case and rejects undefined/malformed values using existing `malformed()`. Add a strict boolean reader. No missing-field defaults and no declaration-based fallback. Frontend `DeclaredPeriodTotal` and `DeclaredHeadlines` types mirror the parsed contract, not an alternate algorithm. Keep formatting as strings.

Files: domain model/service; `inbound/http/handlers/entity_details.rs`; frontend `lib/entity-details.ts`, `lib/server/entity-details.ts`, `lib/member-summary.ts`; existing Rust fixture/tests and frontend specs; one CI workflow; short `AGENTS.md` policy. `MemberIdentity.svelte` should need no substantive changes. Delete `declaredTotal`, its `sumAmounts` import, and frontend `CURRENT_PARLIAMENT_START`. Keep sumAmounts for independent timeline consumers if still used.

Interface depth: two period results hide money, date, category, and completeness policy behind the existing summary response. The frontend sees only display states, without coordinating several calculation helpers. No general-purpose monetary framework or endpoint is needed.

## Verification and CI

Extend existing `details.sql` with one dedicated member, using fixed SQL fixture records:

| Declaration | Registered | Currency/amount | Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | boundary minus one microsecond | GBP 100 | employment |
| 2 | exact boundary | GBP 200 | support |
| 3 | after boundary | GBP 30.25 | gifts |
| 4 | after boundary | GBP -5 | unknown ID 987 |
| 5 | after boundary | GBP 0.10 twice | support |
| 6 | undated | GBP 7.55 | gifts |
| 7 | after boundary | GBP missing | employment |
| 8 | after boundary | unknown currency, known amount | gifts |
| 9 | after boundary | EUR 999 | support |

Hand-derived expected totals: historical `333`, term `225.45`; counts 9 and 7; both incomplete. Employment-only gives 100 and null, support-only gives 200.2 for both, so either category mutation fails. Assert amount exactly, not a frontend-derived expectation. Existing fixtures protect huge decimals, cancellation/zero, negatives and duplicates; add focused assertions for empty member, empty-entry declaration, foreign-only complete/null and missing-only incomplete/null. Do not infer null from zero.

Reuse the real-Axum SQLx test seam already in `outbound/entity_details/tests.rs`. Extend its live HTTP assertions and optionally export the exact successful response bytes for the dedicated member and edge-state members under `EXPOSED_CONTRACT_OUTPUT_DIR`. Export occurs only when explicitly configured; unique fixed filenames, one writer per response, in a fresh temporary directory. The normal Rust test remains independently runnable and asserts fixed expected wire values before writing. The fixture database can then be dropped normally.

Add `frontend/tests/declared-headline-contract.spec.ts` using existing `tests/backend.ts`. In contract mode it reads those exact Rust HTTP payloads and serves them through the existing HTTP stub to the built Svelte application. This exercises actual SQLx records → repository → service → real Rust HTTP serialization → HTTP → strict Svelte server parser → component → browser DOM, without a long-lived Rust server or a second database harness. CI must require the export variable/files and fail if absent; it must never silently skip or use a checked-in handwritten replacement. Ordinary unrelated frontend tests can continue using mocks.

Add a second browser case derived from the exported body: leave authoritative summary intact, replace raw declarations with an empty list or contradictory GBP amount, and assert the same headline values/count-driven state. This intentionally inconsistent payload isolates ownership: any frontend recalculation fails. It is an ownership probe, separate from the unmodified valid integration case. Also remove `declared_totals`, remove amount, and corrupt boolean/date/count separately; assert normal malformed-backend error page, never fallback totals.

One workflow runs for all PRs (simplest reliable triggering; no fragile Rust-only path filtering), with disposable PostgreSQL, Rust, Node 24 and Playwright Chromium. Run schema-backed Rust tests with SQLX_OFFLINE=true and a disposable administrator DATABASE_URL; no importer, source refresh or real development data. Then build/check frontend and run contract plus existing affected tests. Example commands from repo root:

```sh
mkdir -p "$RUNNER_TEMP/exposed-headline-contract"
EXPOSED_CONTRACT_OUTPUT_DIR="$RUNNER_TEMP/exposed-headline-contract" SQLX_OFFLINE=true cargo test -p exposed --lib outbound::entity_details::tests
npm --prefix frontend ci
npm --prefix frontend run check
cd frontend
PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0 npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
EXPOSED_CONTRACT_OUTPUT_DIR="$RUNNER_TEMP/exposed-headline-contract" npm test -- tests/declared-headline-contract.spec.ts tests/member-summary.spec.ts tests/entity-details.spec.ts
```

For local execution substitute a fresh temporary directory for RUNNER_TEMP and supply a local disposable PostgreSQL administrator DATABASE_URL. Verify mutations before completion: temporarily add an employment-only filter before period observation and require the Rust mixed-category assertion to fail; restore. Temporarily reintroduce frontend `declaredTotal` and require the contradictory-payload browser assertion to fail; restore. Record both failures and final passing commands. Mutation scripts need not become a permanent framework. Make the resulting CI check required in branch protection; repository code alone cannot enforce that hosting setting.

Concise policy addition:

> Declared GBP headlines are owned by the backend member summary and include all categories. Frontends display the required authoritative fields and must not recalculate or fall back to declaration sums. Changes to included records/categories, currency, parliamentary boundary, missing-value treatment or labels require an explicit semantic-change note in the PR and corresponding fixed-fixture contract expectations. Do not change expected totals merely to make a test pass.

## Tradeoffs accepted

- Accept ephemeral response export in a test in exchange for reusing SQLx lifecycle and the existing Svelte HTTP harness. It is actual producer output, not a second maintained contract snapshot.
- Accept two uses of one period accumulator in exchange for one implementation of aggregation semantics. Historical headline never performs another monetary sum.
- Accept additive required frontend fields in exchange for fail-closed behavior; deploy backend before frontend if deployments are separate.

## Alternatives considered

1. Long-running fixture Rust API process with Playwright directly attached: equally strong live transport coverage but requires introducing process/database lifecycle coordination already solved by SQLx tests. Prefer only if the export bridge proves cumbersome.
2. Backend formatted labels/HTML: removes formatting from frontend but couples service/API to presentation and widens the contract. Decimal strings plus typed display state are sufficient.
3. Frontend helper plus more unit tests: shortest diff but leaves a second writer for category/date/money rules; fails structural prevention.

## Synthesis decision

Candidate recommendation; orchestrator selects the final base.

## Implementation reconciliation

No implementation performed. Preserve existing boundary semantics, not inferred financial meaning.

## Open questions and risks

Can the repository owner make the new check required? Implementation and CI can proceed independently; report this hosting configuration requirement explicitly. If exported artifacts complicate the existing browser harness, choose the live API alternative instead of weakening to hand-authored payload-only tests.

## Next implementation step

Add the mixed-category fixture and exact HTTP assertions, then extract the shared period accumulator before wiring the strictly required frontend fields.

## Preventing expectation edits from hiding a semantic change

A check that runs only PR-authored assertions is insufficient for the stated agent threat model. After the initial guard lands, keep the small contract dataset and its hand-calculated expectations in a dedicated declarative file, separate from general fixtures (for example `tests/contracts/declared-headlines.json`, containing source records and expected wire/display states). CI obtains this file from the PR's target commit (`github.event.pull_request.base.sha`), passes that base copy to the candidate Rust contract test and browser spec, and refuses to substitute the PR copy. L17: # About protected branches
L18: 
L19: You can protect important branches by setting branch protection rules, which define whether collaborators can delete or force push to the branch and set requirements for any pushes to the branch, such as passing status checks or a linear commit history.
L20: 
L21: Copy markdown
L22: ## Who can use this feature?
L23: 
L24: Protected branches are available in public repositories with GitHub Free and GitHub Free for organizations. Protected branches are also available in public and private repositories with GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Server. See 【4†GitHub's plans】.
L25: 
L26: ## In this article
L27: 
L28:   * 【5†About branch protection rules】
L29: 
L30:   * 【6†About branch protection settings】
L31: ## 【5†About branch protection rules】
L32: 
L33: Tip
L34: 
L35: If you use branch protection rules that require specific status checks, make sure that job names are unique across all workflows. Using the same job name in multiple workflows can cause ambiguous status check results and block pull requests from being merged. See 【7†Status checks】.
L36: You can enforce certain workflows or requirements before a collaborator can push changes to a branch in your repository, including merging a pull request into the branch, by creating a branch protection rule. Actors may only be added to bypass lists when the repository belongs to an organization.
L37: By default, each branch protection rule disables force pushes to the matching branches and prevents the matching branches from being deleted. You can optionally disable these restrictions and enable additional branch protection settings.
L38: By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule don't apply to people with admin permissions to the repository or custom roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission. You can optionally apply the restrictions to administrators and roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission, too. For more information, see 【8†Managing custom repository roles for an organization】.
L39: You can create a branch protection rule in a repository for a specific branch, all branches, or any branch that matches a name pattern you specify with `fnmatch` syntax. For example, to protect any branches containing the word `release`, you can create a branch rule for `*release*`. For more information about branch name patterns, see 【9†Managing a branch protection rule】.
L40: You can configure a pull request to merge automatically when all merge requirements are met. For more information, see 【10†Automatically merging a pull request】.
L41: 
L42: Note
L43: Only a single branch protection rule can apply at a time, which means it can be difficult to know which rule will apply when multiple versions of a rule target the same branch. This restriction does not apply to rulesets, see 【11†About rulesets】. To convert branch protection rules to rulesets, see 【12†Converting branch protections to rulesets】.
L44: ## 【6†About branch protection settings】
L45: 
L46: For each branch protection rule, you can choose to enable or disable the following settings.
L47:   * 【13†Require pull request reviews before merging】
L48:   * 【14†Require status checks before merging】
L49:   * 【15†Require conversation resolution before merging】
L50:   * 【16†Require signed commits】
L51:   * 【17†Require linear history】
L52:   * 【18†Require merge queue】
L53:   * 【19†Require deployments to succeed before merging】
L54:   * 【20†Lock branch】
L55:   * 【21†Do not allow bypassing the above settings】
L56:   * 【22†Restrict who can push to matching branches】
L57:   * 【23†Allow force pushes】
L58:   * 【24†Allow deletions】
L59: For more information on how to set up branch protection, see 【9†Managing a branch protection rule】.
L60: ### 【13†Require pull request reviews before merging】
L61: 
L62: Repository administrators or custom roles with the "edit repository rules" permission can require that all pull requests receive a specific number of approving reviews before someone merges the pull request into a protected branch. You can require approving reviews from people with write permissions in the repository or from a designated code owner.
L63: If you enable required reviews, collaborators can only push changes to a protected branch via a pull request that is approved by the required number of reviewers with write permissions.
L64: 
L65: If a person with admin permissions chooses the Request changes option in a review, then that person must approve the pull request before the pull request can be merged. If a reviewer who requests changes on a pull request isn't available, anyone with write permissions for the repository can dismiss the blocking review.
L66: Even after all required reviewers have approved a pull request, collaborators cannot merge the pull request if there are other open pull requests that have a head branch pointing to the same commit with pending or rejected reviews. Someone with write permissions must approve or dismiss the blocking review on the other pull requests first.
L67: If a collaborator attempts to merge a pull request with pending or rejected reviews into the protected branch, the collaborator will receive an error message.

# Decision

Select **sol** as the implementation base. It removes duplicated historical arithmetic and frontend policy, reuses the existing SQLx lifecycle, and checks real Rust HTTP output through the existing Svelte HTTP test server. Apply the pstack unslop skill to delivery prose.

Scores are judgment on a 1–5 scale, with 5 strongest. The columns follow the requested criteria.

| Candidate | One owner | Exact semantics | PR CI / producer-consumer | Small coherent diff | Expected-value protection |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| sol | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| astra | 5 | 5 | 5 | 3 | 4 |
| luna | 3 | 5 | 4 | 5 | 1 |

Sol's shared `PeriodAggregate::observe` should own the existing currency/category accumulation and coverage rules. Historical headline must read the same GBP aggregate that supplies existing summary currencies. Both periods use this accumulator. Accept unused current-term category aggregates rather than split historical category accumulation back out or create a second GBP-specific reducer. Luna's separate current-term fold would preserve two implementations of monetary/coverage policy; reject it. Astra's live Rust-to-Node process coordinator adds lifecycle and test-selection failure modes without improving the monetary contract enough to justify its scope.

Use sol's exact required response fields and strict frontend parser. Keep normalized decimal strings, null versus zero, inclusive 2024-07-09 midnight UTC, historical-only undated declarations, all categories including unknown IDs, repeated entries, and signed values. Count empty-entry declarations. Unknown currency or missing GBP amount makes the GBP total incomplete; missing foreign-currency amounts do not. Remove the frontend date constant and headline reduction completely. Keep the existing earnings timeline behavior.

# Grafts and practical implementation

1. Adopt astra's explicit ownership documentation and tests for each required field being missing or malformed. A typed term wrapper is optional only if existing domain conventions justify it; one typed boundary function is sufficient here.
2. Keep sol's nine-declaration fixture. Its hand-calculated historical total is `333`, current term is `225.45`, counts are 9 and 7, and both are incomplete. Also test empty, empty-entry, foreign-only, missing-only, exact-zero, and huge-decimal states. Include at least one foreign entry with a missing amount to lock that subtle completeness rule.
3. Use one small versioned `contracts/declared-totals-v1/{fixture.sql,expected.json}` oracle. On PR CI, fetch the exact target commit and materialize its SQL fixture into the SQLx fixture location **before Rust compilation**, along with its expected JSON for both test runners. SQLx embeds fixtures at compilation. Keep this dedicated fixture separate from the ordinary `details.sql` so unrelated records can evolve. Candidate tests must actually read the materialized expected JSON rather than repeat mutable literals elsewhere.
4. Bootstrap v1 only when the target predates the contract's first introduction. Once introduced, missing or partial target files must fail. Define this transition explicitly; a general "missing means use PR files" fallback would let later deletion reset the oracle. An intentional future semantic migration needs explicit baseline review rather than an approval flag or magic label.
5. Have the existing real-Axum SQLx HTTP test assert base-owned expectations and export the successful response bodies to a fresh temporary directory. The contract browser suite must require that directory and expected members, reject absent artifacts, and serve the exact exported bodies through the existing backend stub. Keep a separate contradictory-raw-declarations case to prove summary authority. Do not check in whole API snapshots.
6. Add one workflow running for every PR, with disposable PostgreSQL, Rust, Node, Chromium, strict frontend checks, relevant Rust tests, and the actual contract browser suite. Avoid ignored test orchestration and path filters. Prove an employment-only backend mutation fails and a frontend-recalculation mutation fails; restore both and run the final checks.

# Enforcement limit

Target-owned fixture and expected JSON protect against changing expected amounts in the PR. They do not protect against coordinated changes to the workflow or executable assertions. The repository currently has no effective required checks. Deliver the workflow and name its check, describe that limitation, and leave branch settings unchanged. Required checks and enforced owner review are separate hosting controls for the repository owner.

No repository files were changed during this judgment.

I’m also addressing the “update the expected number until the test passes” problem. CI will use the contract dataset and expected totals from the target branch. Once the baseline is established, changing expected amounts in the same PR won’t hide a regression.

The implementation keeps one backend calculation and removes the competing frontend calculation. Those are the two main protections: fewer places to change the meaning, and an independent check that exposes a change.

Select sol, matching independent cross-judge. One shared backend PeriodAggregate owns exact monetary and coverage rules; historical headline reads same GBP aggregate exposed in existing currency summary. All categories included. Current term adds only inclusive timestamp selection, undated historical only. Required additive declared_totals fields are parsed strictly; frontend passes through rather than computes. Reject separate current-GBP loop and generic category-selectable aggregate API.

Choose SQLx-owned real HTTP response export to existing Svelte HTTP/browser harness over extra live subprocess coordinator. Fixed small versioned SQL fixture plus independently calculated JSON expectations. CI materializes target-commit baseline before compile; only first introduction bootstraps. PR expectation edits therefore do not change regression oracle. A deliberate coordinated edit to workflow/assertions can still bypass this and needs review; do not promise malicious-agent resistance under same owner credentials.

Verification must include two observed failures: backend category filter and frontend recomputation. Final checks cover Rust service/HTTP, strict frontend parser, rendered headlines, existing relevant frontend tests. No migration, import or existing data changes. Source-record updates remain legitimate.

Implementation owner totals_guard_implementation has exclusive worktree. Parent performs independent review, actual-page screenshot/verification, commit/push/PR update, and assesses hosting enforcement only after check exists and succeeds.
EOF","max_output_tokens":1000}));

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  financial-totals-contract:
    name: Financial totals contract
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    services:
      REDACTED:
        image: REDACTED:18
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: REDACTED
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: REDACTED
          POSTGRES_DB: exposed_contract
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U REDACTED"
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
    env:
      DATABASE_URL: REDACTED
      CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG: '0'
      PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH: '0'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Materialize target-branch financial baseline
        env:
          BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          fixture=contracts/declared-totals-v1/fixture.sql
          expected=contracts/declared-totals-v1/expected.json
          has_fixture=false
          has_expected=false
          git cat-file -e "$BASE_SHA:$fixture" 2>/dev/null && has_fixture=true
          git cat-file -e "$BASE_SHA:$expected" 2>/dev/null && has_expected=true
          if "$has_fixture" && "$has_expected"; then
            git show "$BASE_SHA:$fixture" > "$fixture"
            git show "$BASE_SHA:$expected" > "$expected"
            echo "Using frozen financial baseline from target commit $BASE_SHA"
          elif ! "$has_fixture" && ! "$has_expected" &&
               ! git cat-file -e "$BASE_SHA:.github/workflows/financial-totals-contract.yml" 2>/dev/null &&
               ! git cat-file -e "$BASE_SHA:scripts/check-declared-totals-contract.sh" 2>/dev/null; then
            echo 'BOOTSTRAP: target has neither baseline nor financial guard. Reviewing proposed v1 baseline in this PR.'
            test -s "$fixture"
            test -s "$expected"
          else
            echo 'Missing or partial frozen financial baseline on target branch.' >&2
            exit 1
          fi
      - name: Install Rust
        run: |
          rustup toolchain install stable --profile minimal
          rustup default stable
      - uses: actions/setup-node@249970729cb0ef3589644e2896645e5dc5ba9c38
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: frontend/package-lock.json
      - name: Prepare schema for SQLx compile checks
        run: SQLX_OFFLINE=true cargo run --locked -p exposed --bin exposed -- migrate run --source db/migrations
      - name: Install frontend dependencies and Chromium
        run: |
          npm --prefix frontend ci
          cd frontend
          npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Verify fixed backend and rendered financial contract
        run: scripts/check-declared-totals-contract.sh
